---
title: "Install & configure"
---

OMERO-Screen needs three things: the software, a configuration that names your
OMERO server and user, and your password. One command installs the software
and walks you through the rest. Budget ten minutes the first time, most of it
downloading.

## Which install do you need?

| You want to… | Use |
|---|---|
| analyse your plates on a Mac or Linux machine | [Quick install](#quick-install-macos-and-linux) |
| do the same on Windows | [Windows (WSL2)](#windows) |
| run jobs on an HPC cluster | [On an HPC cluster](#on-an-hpc-cluster) |
| try OMERO-Screen without an OMERO account | [Try it locally](try-it.qmd), with a local OMERO server in Docker |
| let Claude run OMERO-Screen for you | the quick install, then [the Claude skills](#quick-install-macos-and-linux) (step 5) |
| change the code | [Developer install](#developer-install) |

## Quick install (macOS and Linux)

Allow about ten minutes, most of it downloading. You need your OMERO user
name and password, and, if your OMERO server is only reachable on the
institute network, the VPN.

**1. Run the installer.** Open **Terminal** and paste:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HocheggerLab/omero-screen/main/install.sh | sh
```

It prints what it does, step by step:

```text
==> Downloading omero-screen-v<version>
==> Installing packages (a few minutes the first time)
Installed … packages in …
==> Compiling Python files for a faster start (quiet; minutes on a laptop, …)
==> Installed omero-screen-v<version> in ~/.local/share/omero-screen/…
fetched nucleitorch_0 …          (the stock Cellpose models)
```

The compile step prints nothing until it is done; let it run. If a download
fails (`could not download …`, `network timeout`), check the network (VPN,
proxy) and run the same line again: it continues where it stopped.

**2. Answer the setup questions.** The installer then runs
`omero-screen setup`:

```text
Site profile (sussex, none) [sussex]:              ← Enter for the Hochegger lab OMERO
OMERO user name: ab123
OMERO password:                                     ← typed blind
Checking the login to ome2.hpc.sussex.ac.uk ...
OK: logged in; your default group is '<your group>'.
Password saved in ~/.config/omero-screen/omero-password (only you can read it).
Wrote ~/.config/omero-screen/config.toml. Next: omero-screen doctor
```

A failed login is almost always the VPN or a typo; run `omero-screen setup`
again. See [Set up your OMERO login](#set-up-your-omero-login) for details.

**3. Read the check.** The installer ends with `omero-screen doctor`. Every
line should say `OK`; `WARN` lines are advice, not failures. Each problem
comes with a `fix:` line.

**4. Open a new Terminal window** if the installer said it updated your
`PATH`, then check the command is found:

```bash
omero-screen --version
```

**5. Add the Claude skills** (optional): they let Claude run OMERO-Screen
for you from plain-language requests ("analyse plate 1234", "plot γH2AX per
siRNA").

- **Claude Code** (terminal, or the desktop app's **Code** tab):

  ```
  /plugin marketplace add HocheggerLab/omero-screen
  /plugin install omero-screen@omero-screen
  ```

  Then switch on updates once: `/plugin` → **Marketplaces** →
  **omero-screen** → auto-update. Updates are off by default for
  marketplaces outside Anthropic's own; without them, update by hand with
  `/plugin marketplace update omero-screen` and `/reload-plugins`.
- **Claude desktop app (chat):** the app does not read marketplaces. Download
  the skills and drag each zip into the app's window for adding a skill:
  [omero-screen.zip](../downloads/omero-screen.zip),
  [cellclass-train.zip](../downloads/cellclass-train.zip),
  [track-review.zip](../downloads/track-review.zip). After an OMERO-Screen
  update, download them again.

What the skills do, and how to use them with other agents:
[Agent skills](agent-skills.qmd) and [Working with Claude](claude.qmd).

You are ready for [your first plate](first-plate.qmd).

### What the installer does

1. installs [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), which brings its own Python, if
   it is missing;
2. downloads the latest release and installs exactly the tested versions of
   everything, including napari, CellView, cellclass and the plotting
   library, into `~/.local/share/omero-screen`;
3. puts the commands (`omero-screen`, `cellview`, `cellclass`, `napari`, …) in
   uv's command directory (normally `~/.local/bin`) and adds that directory to
   your shell `PATH` automatically if needed (you do not need to edit `.zshrc`
   yourself);
4. downloads the stock Cellpose segmentation models, so a network problem
   shows up now rather than in the middle of your first plate;
5. runs `omero-screen setup` and `omero-screen doctor`.

### Installer options

Set these as environment variables before `sh`, for example
`curl … | OMERO_SCREEN_NO_SETUP=1 sh`:

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `OMERO_SCREEN_VERSION` | install this release tag (e.g. `omero-screen-v0.10.4`) instead of the latest |
| `OMERO_SCREEN_HOME` | install here instead of `~/.local/share/omero-screen` (e.g. a project space with more room) |
| `OMERO_SCREEN_BIN` | link the commands here instead of uv's command directory; your `PATH` is then not changed |
| `OMERO_SCREEN_NO_SETUP=1` | skip `omero-screen setup` and `doctor` at the end |
| `OMERO_SCREEN_BRANCH` | install a branch instead of a release (for testing changes) |
| `OMERO_SCREEN_HEADLESS` | `1`: install without the napari GUI; `0`: with it. By default the install is headless on an HPC cluster (SLURM present) or with glibc older than 2.34, and has the GUI elsewhere. An update keeps the choice of the install it replaces |
| `UV_HTTP_TIMEOUT` | download timeout in seconds; the installer uses 300 unless you set it (uv's own 30 s is too short behind some proxies) |
| `UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE_TIMEOUT` | per-file compile timeout in seconds; the installer uses 600 unless you set it (uv's own 60 s is too short on a busy cluster filesystem) |

### What goes where

| What | Where | Size |
|---|---|---|
| The software: one folder per release, each with its own Python environment | `~/.local/share/omero-screen/<release>`, with `current` pointing at the one in use | ~2.3 GB per release, two kept |
| The commands | `~/.local/bin` (links into `current`) | — |
| Your settings | `~/.config/omero-screen/config.toml` | — |
| Your password | `~/.config/omero-screen/omero-password`, readable only by you | — |
| Cellpose models | `~/.cellpose/models` | 25 MB per Cellpose 3 model; 1.2 GB for Cellpose 4 (`cpsam`) |
| Downloaded images | `~/omero-cache` | grows with use |
| CellView database | `~/.cellview/cellview.duckdb` | grows with use |
| Downloaded packages, reused by updates | uv's cache (`uv cache dir`) | shared by all releases |

The two releases on disk share most of their files with uv's cache, so they
take less space than `du` reports, as long as the cache is on the same disk.

### Windows {#windows}

The installer is a shell script, and the local OMERO server needs Docker, which
on Windows runs on WSL2 anyway, so on Windows OMERO-Screen runs inside WSL2
(a Linux system built into Windows):

1. In PowerShell, run `wsl --install`, restart, and create a Linux user when
   Ubuntu opens.
2. In the Ubuntu window, run the [quick install](#quick-install-macos-and-linux)
   line.
3. For [Try it locally](try-it.qmd), install
   [Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/windows-install/)
   and turn on *Settings → Resources → WSL integration* for Ubuntu.

napari opens as a normal window on Windows 11.

::: {.callout-note}
The Windows route has not yet been tested end to end. Please report problems
as a GitHub issue.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
If you work with Claude, continue with [Working with Claude](claude.qmd) once
the installer has finished.
:::

## Update

```bash
omero-screen self update            # install the latest release
omero-screen self update --check    # only say whether there is one
```

Your settings and data are kept. `omero-screen doctor` also tells you when a
newer release is out. Running the install line again does the same as
`self update`.

The previous release stays on disk, so you can go back if a new one causes
trouble; older releases are removed (each takes several GB):

```bash
omero-screen self update --version 0.8.27
```

## Uninstall

```bash
omero-screen self uninstall           # remove the software and its commands
omero-screen self uninstall --purge   # also your settings and password file
```

What each operation does with the things listed in
[What goes where](#what-goes-where):

| | Update | Uninstall | Uninstall `--purge` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Software (current release) | replaced by the new one | removed | removed |
| Previous release | kept for rollback; older ones removed | removed | removed |
| Commands in `~/.local/bin` | relinked | removed (only ours) | removed (only ours) |
| Settings (`config.toml`) | kept | kept | **removed** |
| Password file (and a keychain entry from an older setup) | kept | kept | **removed** |
| Cellpose models, image cache, CellView database | kept | kept, listed | kept, listed |
| uv and its cache | kept | kept | kept |

Only commands that link into the install are removed; a `napari` you
installed yourself stays. Your data (the CellView database, the image cache
and the Cellpose models) is never deleted, not even with `--purge`: the
uninstaller lists where it is so you can delete it yourself.
`uv self uninstall` removes uv.

If the `omero-screen` command no longer works, uninstall from the web:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HocheggerLab/omero-screen/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall
```

## Set up your OMERO login

```bash
omero-screen setup
```

It asks for:

- the **site profile**: a ready-made description of your server and
  microscopes. Choose `sussex` for the Hochegger lab OMERO, or `none` to type
  in a server name;
- your **OMERO user name** and **password**. The password is checked against
  the server, then saved in `~/.config/omero-screen/omero-password`, a file
  only you can read. The same on every machine (Mac, Linux, WSL, an HPC
  cluster), and nothing asks for it again;
- on an **HPC cluster**, where to put the **image cache**. It can grow to
  tens of GB, so setup suggests your work space (on the Sussex HPC, your
  Lustre folder) rather than your home directory.

Your answers are saved in `~/.config/omero-screen/config.toml`; the password
never is. Run `setup` again at any time to change them: settings it doesn't
ask about (model sets, paths, stitch overrides) are kept.

## Check the installation

```bash
omero-screen doctor
```

`doctor` checks everything OMERO-Screen needs (the software, your login, the
connection to the server, CellView, napari, the GPU and disk space) and says
how to fix anything that fails. If something does not work, run it first. A
failed connection is usually the VPN.

```bash
omero-screen config show      # the settings in effect, and where each came from
omero-screen --version        # the installed version
```

## Hardware

Segmentation and tracking are the expensive steps. Everything runs on a
laptop; some combinations need the right hardware.

| | Apple silicon (MPS) | NVIDIA (CUDA) | CPU only |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Default segmentation** | stock Cellpose 3 models (`nuclei`, `cyto3`) | Cellpose 4 (`cpsam`) | stock Cellpose 3, slow |
| **Cellpose 4** (`--cp4`) | not in practice: too slow and too large | yes | impractical |
| **Tracking** (`--track`) | falls back to CPU | yes | slow |
| **Classifier inference** | yes | yes | workable |

- **Segmentation models.** With no models configured, OMERO-Screen picks the
  best default for the machine and says so in the log. The stock Cellpose 3
  models segment most cells reasonably; a model trained on your own cells and
  microscope does better: see [Make a model for your cells](models.qmd).
- **The models used are recorded on every plate.** Each run writes the
  version, settings, device and models onto the plate in OMERO, so you can
  always tell how a plate was segmented.
- **Tracking has no MPS backend.** On Apple silicon, `--track` runs on the
  CPU: correct, but slow.

Device selection is automatic: CUDA if present, then MPS, then CPU. Force CPU
with `OMERO_SCREEN_USE_GPU=0`.

## On an HPC cluster

On a cluster you install once on a **login node**, and every analysis runs as
a **SLURM job** on a GPU node: never run the pipeline on the login node. The
steps below use the Sussex HPC (Artemis) as the example; on another cluster
the folder names differ.

**1. Log in to a login node** and find your two storage areas: your home
directory (small, often a slow shared NFS) and your work space for large data
(on Artemis, Lustre: `/mnt/lustre/users/<group>/$USER`).

**2. Choose where the software goes.** It is ~2.3 GB in tens of thousands of
small files. Put it on the **same filesystem as uv's download cache**:
uv then hardlinks files from the cache instead of copying them.

```bash
uv cache dir          # without uv yet: it will be ~/.cache/uv
```

Put both in your work space and make it permanent. If `uv cache dir` already
points into your work space, keep it and only set `OMERO_SCREEN_HOME`:

```bash
W=/mnt/lustre/users/<group>/$USER                    # your work space
echo "export UV_CACHE_DIR=$W/.cache/uv" >> ~/.bashrc
echo "export OMERO_SCREEN_HOME=$W/omero-screen-install" >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
```

Don't point `OMERO_SCREEN_HOME` at a source checkout. If install and cache are
on different filesystems, uv warns `Failed to hardlink files` and copies
everything: on Artemis that took 45 minutes instead of under 2.

**3. Run the installer** on the login node:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HocheggerLab/omero-screen/main/install.sh | sh
```

It sees SLURM and installs **headless**: everything except the napari GUI,
which a cluster doesn't need:

```text
==> Headless install, without the napari GUI (SLURM cluster); OMERO_SCREEN_HEADLESS=0 adds it
==> Installing packages (a few minutes the first time)
Installed 222 packages in 1m 46s
==> Compiling Python files for a faster start (quiet; … up to half an hour on a busy cluster filesystem)
Bytecode compiled 16650 files in 15m 14s
```

The compile is slow on a cluster filesystem (every file is a round trip to a
shared server) but saves every job from doing it. If it stops with a timeout,
run the same line again: installed packages are kept.

**4. Answer the setup questions**, as on a laptop, plus one:

```text
Site profile (sussex, none) [sussex]:
OMERO user name: ab123
OMERO password:
OK: logged in; your default group is '<your group>'.
Password saved in ~/.config/omero-screen/omero-password (only you can read it).
Image cache folder (can grow to tens of GB; …) [/mnt/lustre/users/<group>/ab123/omero-cache]:
```

Accept the suggested image cache in your work space: downloaded images can
grow to tens of GB and do not belong in home.

**5. Read the check.** `doctor` should report `OK` everywhere except
`napari and Qt` (a warning on a headless install) and the compute device,
which is `CPU only` on a login node; the GPU is checked in step 7.

**6. Fetch the models once, on the login node,** so that parallel jobs don't
all download them at the same time. The stock models came with the
installer; for the lab's own models:

```bash
omero-screen models pull hocheggerlab
```

and set `model_set = "hocheggerlab"` under `[segmentation]` in
`~/.config/omero-screen/config.toml`. On a GPU node with no model set, the
default is Cellpose 4 (`cpsam`), which downloads on first use (1.2 GB).

**7. Test a GPU node** with a 10-minute job that only runs the check:

```bash
cd /mnt/lustre/users/<group>/$USER
sbatch -p gpu --gres=gpu:1 --mem=8G --time=00:10:00 -o doctor-%j.out \
  --wrap "$(command -v omero-screen) doctor"
squeue -u $USER                  # wait until the job has gone
cat doctor-*.out
```

Look for `Compute device: CUDA …` and `OMERO connection: connected`. The
PyTorch build needs an NVIDIA driver for CUDA 12 (driver 525 or newer).

**8. Submit plates** from your work space with `omero-screen-sbatch`:

```bash
cd /mnt/lustre/users/<group>/$USER
omero-screen-sbatch 12345 --no-submit     # writes the job script only: check it
omero-screen-sbatch 12345                 # submit; one job per plate
omero-screen-sbatch 12345 67890 --stitch --track
squeue -u $USER
```

Each job checks the GPU first, runs the pipeline with the options you gave,
logs to `os<plate>.<pid>.<jobid>.out` in that folder, and e-mails
`<your login>@sussex.ac.uk` when it ends (`-u` changes the login). Job options (memory, hours, partition) are in
[Running on a SLURM cluster](hpc.qmd).

**9. Update** on the login node, as anywhere else:

```bash
omero-screen self update
```

The install stays where `OMERO_SCREEN_HOME` put it. Jobs that are already
queued keep the release they were submitted with until it is removed (the
previous release is kept, so wait for running jobs before updating twice).

**10. Claude on the cluster** (optional): with Claude Code on the login
node, add the plugin as in [step 5 of the quick install](#quick-install-macos-and-linux).
The skills know the cluster rules: Claude checks the install and submits
plates with `omero-screen-sbatch`, and never runs the pipeline or training on
the login node.

### When something goes wrong on the cluster

| You see | Meaning | Do |
|---|---|---|
| `Failed to hardlink files; falling back to full copy` | install and uv's cache on different filesystems | install beside the cache (step 2) |
| `Failed to download … network timeout` | the proxy was slow | run the install line again (the installer already allows 300 s) |
| `Bytecode timed out` | the filesystem stalled on one file | run the install line again |
| The installer seems stuck after `Installed … packages` | it is compiling, quietly | wait; `top -u $USER` shows `python` working |
| `Compute device: CPU only` in a job | the job did not get a GPU | ask for one: `-p gpu --gres=gpu:1` |
| `OMERO login incomplete` in a job | no user config for this account | run `omero-screen setup` on the login node |

## The configuration in detail

Settings come from several places. A value set higher up in this list wins:

1. command-line flags (e.g. `--cp4`);
2. environment variables (`HOST`, `USERNAME`, `OMERO_SCREEN_*`);
3. a `.env` file in a source checkout (developers, see below);
4. your **user config**, `~/.config/omero-screen/config.toml`;
5. the **site profile** it names;
6. built-in defaults.

A user config written by `setup` looks like this:

```toml
site = "sussex"

[omero]
username = "ab123"
# group = "my-lab-group"          # default: your OMERO default group

[segmentation]
# model_set = "hocheggerlab"      # the lab's models; first: omero-screen models pull hocheggerlab

[paths]
# cache = "~/omero-cache"         # downloaded images
# cellview_db = "~/.cellview/cellview.duckdb"

[env]
# any OMERO_SCREEN_* variable, e.g.
# OMERO_SCREEN_USE_GPU = "0"
```

A **site profile** holds what everyone at a site shares: the OMERO server and
port, the stitch calibrations of its microscopes, its model sets. `sussex` is
built in. For another site, write one as a TOML file, set
`site = "/path/to/your-site.toml"`, and send it to us so it can be included.

`setup` writes the password file for you. To use a file you made yourself
instead, put the password in a file only you can read and name it in the user
config (or run `omero-screen setup --password-file <file>`, which does both):

```bash
umask 077 && echo 'your-password' > ~/.omero-password
```

```toml
[omero]
password_file = "~/.omero-password"
```

The `PASSWORD` environment variable works too, and takes precedence.

Setups made before the password file kept the password in the system
keychain. It is still read until you run `omero-screen setup` again, and
`doctor` warns about it; after that you can delete the old entry with
`security delete-generic-password -s omero-screen` (macOS).

## Working in another user's screens

To analyse plates that belong to someone else, you need at least read access
to their OMERO group. Your OMERO administrator sets this. Masks and results
are written to your own `Screens` project.

## Developer install

To work on the code, clone the repository and install the workspace with the
development tools:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/HocheggerLab/omero-screen.git
cd omero-screen
uv sync --dev
uv run omero-screen doctor
```

`uv sync` installs all six packages (the core pipeline, `cellview`,
`omero-screen-plots`, `omero-screen-napari`, `cellclass` and `omero-utils`).
Configure with `uv run omero-screen setup` as above. A `.env.development` (or
`.env.production`, selected with `ENV=production`) at the repository root is
still read and takes precedence over the user config:

```bash
USERNAME="your-omero-login"
PASSWORD="your-omero-password"
HOST="omero.your-institution.ac.uk"
```

::: {.callout-warning}
`.env.*` files hold your password in plain text. They are gitignored; keep it
that way, and never paste one into an issue or a pull request.
:::

Run `uv run omero-integration-test e2e_connection` to check the connection to
a test server.

### A release and a checkout side by side

You can keep the installed release for day-to-day work and a checkout for
development. They use separate Python environments: inside the checkout,
`uv run omero-screen` (or the checkout's activated `.venv`) runs your
development code; elsewhere, `omero-screen` runs the release. Check which one
you have with `omero-screen --version`.

They share your settings, password file, Cellpose models, image cache and
CellView database. Two things to watch:

- **`.env` files.** Any `omero-screen` command reads the `.env.{ENV}` file
  (default `.env.development`) of the git repository containing the current
  folder. Run inside your checkout, the release therefore uses the checkout's
  development settings. Run the release from outside any repository with a
  `.env` file.
- **Shared data.** Point the checkout at its own CellView database
  (`DATABASE_PATH` in `.env.development`) so experiments don't touch the one
  you work with.
